--------
In this VladTV interview, Marlow Bates and Tamir Stanfield reflect on seeing HBO’s *The Wire* premiere in 2002 while they were incarcerated, and respond to the long-running belief that elements of the Baltimore crime drama were inspired by their lives. They discuss creator David Simon, former detective Ed Burns, and the Season 3 introduction of Marlo Stanfield, played by Jamie Hector. Bates explains how his name and reputation were connected to the character, while disputing key storylines involving Omar, children selling drugs, and the infamous candy-store scene. Stanfield adds that many names and situations in the series felt connected to real people, despite being presented as fiction. The conversation offers rare firsthand perspective on Baltimore street history, media portrayal, and how *The Wire* continues to shape conversations about crime, television, and real-life inspiration.

--------
John Franzese Jr. sits down with Vlad to recount the early 1990s, a period marked by family turmoil, addiction, homelessness, and a life-changing HIV diagnosis. He reflects on Michael Franzese’s 1991 arrest by U.S. Marshals in Bel Air over alleged loan and rental fraud, probation issues, tax filings, and a disputed check, while describing his own years in New York subway tunnels, crack addiction, overdoses, and failed attempts to get clean in Los Angeles areas like Wilshire and Brentwood.  

Franzese explains how a blood test through his family doctors revealed he was HIV positive in 1989 or 1990, before Magic Johnson’s announcement changed public awareness of HIV/AIDS. He discusses the fear surrounding AIDS at the time, early Western Blot testing, stigma, disclosure to partners, support from siblings including Michael, Tina, Lorraine, and Cammy, and warnings involving the FBI.

--------

Tito “TJ” Dominguez sits down with VladTV to reflect on a pivotal moment in narco history: the 1993 death of Pablo Escobar, killed in Colombia by a joint Colombian and American task force while Dominguez was serving a federal prison sentence. Rather than celebrating or mourning the Medellín Cartel leader’s fall, Dominguez says he was focused on his own survival, family, and future—summarizing the moment as “the king is dead, long live the king.”

After his release on parole, Dominguez recalls the FBI warning him about a list of names tied to his past, making it clear they would come for him if anything happened. He describes trying to leave the streets behind after becoming a father, while clashing with a parole officer determined to send him back to prison.

A candid look at crime, consequences, Escobar’s legacy, and life after federal prison.

Chris Feistl joins Vlad to break down the rise of Colombia’s Cali Cartel after the fall of Pablo Escobar and the Medellin Cartel. The conversation traces the roots of the cartel war, from Medellin’s push into New York cocaine territory to the failed 1989 Monaco building bombing targeting Escobar’s family. Feistl details how Los Pepes, Fidel Castaño, Carlos Castaño, Don Berna, and the Colombian National Police Search Bloc helped corner Escobar before his death in Medellin.

The interview also examines how the Cali Cartel quietly expanded while Escobar battled the Colombian government, following attacks tied to Luis Carlos Galán, Avianca, and the DAS headquarters. With Miami, New York, Colombia, Spain, and Europe as key trafficking corridors, Feistl explains how Cali used bribery, political influence, and global infrastructure to dominate the cocaine trade after 1994.

--------
In this VladTV interview, former Mexican Mafia member Rene “Boxer” Enriquez breaks down the real economics behind La Eme during the early years of its prison “taxation” and extortion program. Speaking candidly about life inside Pelican Bay State Prison, Enriquez says he was making roughly $50,000 to $80,000 a year from collections—serious money in his world, but far from the fortunes associated with Pablo Escobar, Carlos Lehder, Freeway Ricky Ross, the Italian mob, Hells Angels, Aryan Brotherhood, or the Yakuza.  

Enriquez explains why older Mexican Mafia rules discouraged members from using the organization to get rich, how that changed over time, and why substance abuse, life sentences, internal politics, and a lack of centralized leadership have limited La Eme’s growth. A revealing look at prison gangs, organized crime, extortion, power, and survival from someone who witnessed the system from the inside.
